C1 Mon 31 Aug 07:10 IST, C2 Tue 1 Sep 07:10, C3 Wed 2 Sep 21:15, C4 batch 1 Thu 3 Sep 07:10, batch 2 Mon 7 Sep 07:10, batch 3 Wed 9 Sep 07:10. 07:10 is the pre-OPD phone check before ward rounds, the single highest-intent inbox moment for an Indian clinician; 21:15 is after evening OPD and dinner, which suits the cohort that reads long but acts slowly. Nothing sends between 11:00 and 16:00 IST (OPD and theatre). Minutes are set to :10 because runDueCampaigns polls every 60 seconds, so a :00 target can slip.
stages.audience: Four static lists, built pre-flight. C1 Attendees, approx 230, from the 27 June Zoom attendee log deduped and matched to the list. C2 Registered-no-shows, approx 170, Zoom registrant export minus attendee log. C3 Prior engaged non-registrants, approx 400, from the Postmark Activity export if it can be pulled; if it cannot, this cohort does not exist and folds into C4. C4 Cold remainder, approx 2,560 to 2,960, horizon-clean.csv minus the other three, minus UNDELIVERABLE verdicts.
stages.entryCondition: Subscriber.status = SUBSCRIBED, not in global_suppression, and verification_result.verdict is not UNDELIVERABLE (queueFromList enforces both automatically). Cohort membership decided once, pre-flight, and frozen for the flow.
stages.exitCondition: CampaignRecipient.status = SENT for that cohort's campaign, or SKIPPED/FAILED. Cohort exits the stage 96 hours after its send, when the branch sets are cut.

branches.measuredHow: No automation exists. A human unlocks the mailbox (POST /api/mail/unlock) and reads GET /api/mail/messages once each morning; set Campaign.replyTo to a single monitored address so replies do not scatter. Log the reply against the person by hand. The permanent fix is the VERP build gap: per-recipient Reply-To of reply+{token}@jarurat.care in SesSender.build, which needs no header threading.
branches.goesTo: Stage 4 immediately, and out of the automated stream until a human has answered
branches.waitBefore: Zero wait. A reply is checked and routed the same working day, because reply latency is the one variable that visibly changes conversion on a peer-to-peer clinical list.

branches.measuredHow: tracking_event WHERE campaign_id = <stage 1 campaign> AND event_type = 'CLICK' AND classification = 'HUMAN', joined to subscriber for the email set. There is no endpoint that returns this set (SubscriberRepository.search filters only q/status/listId), so this is a psql query on the Postgres box at mailer.jarurat.care, or the SegmentResolver build gap. Aggregate sanity check with GET /api/analytics/links?campaignId=.
branches.goesTo: Warm branch: gets the warm copy cut at Stage 3 and is exempt from Stage 5b forever
branches.waitBefore: 72 hours. Clicks cluster in the first 36 hours but a Wednesday send picks up a real Saturday tail on this audience.

branches.measuredHow: tracking_event WHERE event_type='OPEN' AND classification='HUMAN' AND campaign_id=<stage 1>, minus the click set. Do NOT use CampaignRecipient.openedAt for this: OpenTrackingService.java:118-122 documents that the legacy column is never retro-corrected and it counts Apple MPP and bot fetches. Run POST /api/analytics/reclassify before cutting the set.
branches.goesTo: Default path: Stage 2, then the cold copy cut at Stage 3
branches.waitBefore: 96 hours. Anything shorter systematically misclassifies clinicians on a weekend-reading pattern as non-openers, which is the single most common way a flow like this poisons its own branch data.

branches.measuredHow: The cohort's recipient set (GET /api/campaigns/{id}/export?status=SENT) minus the HUMAN open set from tracking_event. Silence counter incremented by 1 for that subscriber, tracked in your own sheet since the platform has no such field.
branches.goesTo: Stays in the flow through Stage 3 and gets exactly one retry at Stage 5b; the counter feeds Stage 8
branches.waitBefore: 96 hours, same reason as above.

branches.measuredHow: GET /api/subscribers?status=BOUNCED and GET /api/suppressions?q=. Attribution to the campaign is a documented heuristic in AnalyticsAggregateRepository.java:64-83, so read it as a batch-level number, not a per-person truth. Note the SNS webhook is inert (jarurat.sns.allowed-topic-arns is unset, every POST /api/sns/ses-events returns 403), so the live path is the 15-minute SES suppression poll. Allow 30 minutes after a send before reading.
branches.goesTo: Auto-suppressed by SuppressionService. Any single domain reaching 5 or more bounces gets removed at domain level by hand before the next batch.
branches.waitBefore: 24 hours for the batch verdict, and a hard gate before the next warm-up batch fires.

stages.successMetric: Per cohort, HUMAN open rate (not the inflated legacy number). C1 45-55% and 12-18% click; C2 35-45% and 8-12%; C3 22-30% and 4-6%; C4 12-18% and 1.0-2.0%. A good cold-cohort number on an 88% freemail Indian doctor list is 15% HUMAN open, which will display as roughly 28-33% unfiltered, and the gap between those two is the inflationFactor AnalyticsService already prints. Batch 1 bounce under 4%, batches 2 and 3 under 1.5%, complaint under 0.05%, unsubscribe 0.3-0.8%.
stages.killCriteria: Do not fire batch 2 or 3 if batch 1 shows bounce above 4% or complaint above 0.08%; re-verify the remaining cold list instead. SafetyCheckService blocks at 5.0% bounce and 0.5% complaint, which is far too lax for Gmail's 0.10% bulk-sender line, so set your own gate. Do not run Stage 1 at all if GET /api/overview shows DKIM or MAIL FROM unverified on horizonevent.info. Do not send C4 before C1 and C2 have landed cleanly: sequence is the warm-up. Skip any cohort whose event date or faculty is not yet confirmed.
stages.teachingNote: A first email is not an announcement, it is a re-introduction, and what needs re-introducing depends entirely on what the person did last time. Three side notes the team must internalise. One: campaign subject lines are sent raw (CampaignService.sendOne passes getSubject() straight to SES with no merge pass), so a {{FIRST_NAME}} in a subject ships literally to 3,363 doctors. Two: only NAME, FIRST_NAME and EMAIL resolve, everything else renders as an empty string. Three: the 12 blank-first-name rows in horizon-clean.csv would render 'Dear ,' so they get their own micro-list and a no-name opening. And warm-up order is free cohort logic: doing it in engagement order costs nothing and buys deliverability.

stages.name: The Give (no ask, no registration link)
stages.purpose: Deliver something genuinely useful with zero request attached, so that Stage 3's ask is a second interaction rather than a first, and so that the click signal it produces measures interest in the subject matter rather than interest in a free seat.
stages.timing: T-14, Sat 12 Sep 2026, 11:00 IST. Saturday late morning is the only unhurried reading window this audience reliably has, and it is the slot where a long-form clinical piece actually gets read rather than triaged. Fourteen days before the event is deliberate: far enough out that no reasonable reader suspects a setup, close enough that the topic is still live when the ask lands 72 hours later.
stages.audience: Everyone delivered in Stage 1 and not suppressed, all four cohorts, approximately 3,290. Registrants who already signed up off-list are excluded and go straight to the registrant track.
stages.entryCondition: CampaignRecipient.status = SENT on any Stage 1 campaign, and email not in global_suppression at queue time.
stages.exitCondition: Sent. Every recipient continues to Stage 3 regardless of behaviour; this stage never removes anyone.

branches.signal: HUMAN click on the give asset
branches.measuredHow: tracking_event WHERE campaign_id=<stage 2> AND event_type='CLICK' AND classification='HUMAN'. Because per-link attribution is by destination URL string only (there are no link IDs or labels), give the recording link and the takeaway PDF distinct UTM-tagged URLs or GET /api/analytics/links cannot tell them apart.
branches.goesTo: Warm branch, merged with Stage 1 clickers. Gets the warm copy at Stage 3 and is a Stage 4 candidate.
branches.waitBefore: 72 hours. This is the last branch cut before Stage 3, so it must be closed by Mon 14 Sep evening.

branches.measuredHow: tracking_event OPEN/HUMAN for the stage 2 campaign minus its click set, after POST /api/analytics/reclassify.
branches.goesTo: Stage 3 cold copy cut
branches.waitBefore: 72 hours.

branches.signal: Silent on both Stage 1 and Stage 2
branches.measuredHow: Set difference: Stage 1 recipient export minus the union of HUMAN opens on both stage campaigns in tracking_event. Silence counter goes to 2.
branches.goesTo: Stage 3, then Stage 5b, then the Stage 8 candidate pool
branches.waitBefore: 72 hours.

branches.measuredHow: global_suppression WHERE reason='UNSUBSCRIBED', via GET /api/suppressions. Enforced at queue time, send time and suppression time, so no manual action is needed.
branches.goesTo: Out of the flow permanently
branches.waitBefore: Immediate and automatic.

stages.successMetric: 18-24% HUMAN open and 3-5% click, which should beat the same cohort's Stage 3 ask by roughly 4-7 percentage points on opens. The number that actually matters here is unsubscribe: it should be under 0.3%, materially lower than any ask email in the flow. If a give email drives unsubscribes at ask-email rates, the give is not valued and the asset needs replacing, not the copy.
stages.killCriteria: Do not send this stage if the asset is not finished, hosted and clicked-through by a human that morning. A give email with a dead link is worse than no email at all, because it spends the reciprocity and returns nothing. Do not sneak a registration CTA in, not even in the footer; the moment it contains an ask it stops being this stage and Stage 3 loses its foundation. Skip anyone who has already registered. Skip anyone who received three emails in the previous seven days.
stages.teachingNote: This is the stage a marketing team will always want to cut, and cutting it is why two-email campaigns plateau. An ask sent to someone who has received nothing from you is a cold ask; the same ask sent 72 hours after something they found useful is a warm one, and the difference shows up in click rate, not open rate. There is a measurement dividend too: a click here is uncontaminated by the offer, so it is the cleanest interest signal in the whole flow and it is what makes Stage 4's audience worth a human's time.

stages.name: The Ask (registration opens)
stages.purpose: Make the single clearest registration request of the flow, in two copy cuts, and produce the first real conversion measurement.
stages.timing: T-11, Tue 15 Sep 2026, 07:10 IST. Tuesday because Monday morning is OPD backlog and nothing gets read; eleven days out because that is long enough for a consultant to move a Saturday evening but short enough that the date feels real. Seventy-two hours after the give, which is the shortest gap that does not read as a bait-and-switch.
stages.audience: Every non-registrant, approximately 3,150, split into two campaigns: WARM (clicked Stage 1 or Stage 2, roughly 450) and COLD (opened only, or silent, roughly 2,700). Two campaigns because the platform has no variant column, so a copy cut is literally a separate campaign against a separate list.
stages.entryCondition: Not present in the Zoom registrant export as of the morning of the send, and not suppressed.
stages.exitCondition: Registered (leaves for the registrant track and Stage 6b), or replied (leaves for Stage 4), or continues to Stage 5.

branches.measuredHow: Zoom API GET /meetings/{id}/registrants exported to CSV, the same call send_emails.py already makes for its exclusion step. This is ground truth. The platform's own proxy is a HUMAN click on the registration URL in tracking_event, which measures intent and overstates completion by roughly 25-40%. GET /api/mailer/success records nothing today; the small build gap that fixes this properly is accepting ?token= on that endpoint and writing a conversion_event row.
branches.goesTo: Registrant track: skips Stages 5 and 6a entirely, receives Stage 6b, day-of reminders, and Stage 7a or 7b
branches.waitBefore: Pull the registrant export every morning at 09:00 IST for the rest of the flow. Never send an ask to someone who registered yesterday.

branches.signal: Clicked the registration link but did not register
branches.measuredHow: tracking_event CLICK/HUMAN on the registration URL for the stage 3 campaign, minus the Zoom registrant export. This is the highest-value non-converting group in the entire flow.
branches.goesTo: Stage 4 personal email, and Stage 6a last chance
branches.waitBefore: 48 hours. Registration abandonment on a Zoom form is almost always same-session; after two days it is a decision, not a delay.

branches.measuredHow: tracking_event OPEN/HUMAN for the stage 3 campaign minus its click set.
branches.goesTo: Stage 5a, agenda and faculty depth
branches.waitBefore: 96 hours, closing Sat 19 Sep morning so Stage 5a can send the same day.

branches.measuredHow: GET /api/campaigns/{id}/export?status=SENT for the stage 3 campaigns, minus the HUMAN open set in tracking_event. Silence counter goes to 3.
branches.goesTo: Stage 5b, the single permitted retry
branches.waitBefore: 96 hours.

branches.measuredHow: Monitored replyTo inbox via GET /api/mail/messages, human-checked twice daily during the ask window.
branches.goesTo: Stage 4 human track
branches.waitBefore: Zero.

stages.successMetric: COLD cut 16-22% HUMAN open, 2.5-4.0% registration-link click. WARM cut 30-38% open, 9-14% click. Net new registrations from this stage 90-140, which on a 3,363 list is 2.7-4.2%. For context, the June run had 163 registrants on the board at send time against 3,367 emailed, about 3.8%, so a good single ask email roughly matches what the entire previous two-email campaign produced.
stages.killCriteria: Do not send if the Zoom registration URL is not live and tested from a phone that morning, or if faculty confirmation is not in writing. A dead or wrong link on the primary ask is the one failure the rest of the flow cannot compensate for. Do not send the WARM cut to anyone who has not actually clicked anything, no matter how much you want the bigger warm number. Do not send at all to anyone already in the registrant export.
stages.teachingNote: One ask, one link, one date, one action. The layered value stack goes inside the body (senior hook in the first two lines, trainee hook mid, student hook last) precisely because the list has no seniority tagging, and never as 'Dear Doctor'. Note what the platform costs you here: with no variant column and no cohort column, a two-cut send means two campaigns over two hand-split lists, and GET /api/analytics/campaigns compares them only whole-to-whole. At roughly 1,300 per arm on a 16% base, the smallest difference you can honestly detect is about 3 percentage points, so only test big swings in subject-line style and never micro-copy.

stages.name: The Reply Loop (personal ask, human routing, 24h SLA)
stages.purpose: Convert the highest-intent non-registrants through a human conversation rather than a broadcast, and stand up the reply-handling machinery that runs continuously underneath every other stage.
stages.timing: The send is T-9, Thu 17 Sep 2026, 21:15 IST, plain-text-style, from a named person, short. Evening because a reply-inviting email needs to arrive when the reader has three unhurried minutes, not between patients. The handling layer runs continuously from Day 1 to E+10, with inbox checks at 09:00 and 18:00 IST every working day.
stages.audience: Engaged but unregistered, approximately 450: anyone who clicked at Stage 1, 2 or 3 but is absent from the Zoom registrant export. Plus, as a separate manual cut, the 60-80 most senior identifiable contacts, who get a peer-to-peer version sent from a clinician team member's own clinical address rather than through JCF-Mailer at all.
stages.entryCondition: At least one HUMAN click in the flow, no registration, not suppressed, and no reply already in progress.
stages.exitCondition: Replied and answered by a human, or registered, or 96 hours elapsed with neither, in which case they continue to Stage 6a.

branches.signal: Replied with a question or interest
branches.measuredHow: The monitored replyTo mailbox read through GET /api/mail/messages and GET /api/mail/search. There is no automated match to a campaign: MessageSummary carries no In-Reply-To, CampaignRecipient.messageId is never searched, there is no REPLIED status, and MailboxAccess keeps the mailbox secret in a browser HttpSession so no background job can even read the inbox. Until the VERP build gap ships (per-recipient Reply-To reply+{token}@, which needs no header threading), matching is by sender address against the recipient export, done by a human.
branches.goesTo: Human owner within one business day, then a manual track outside the automated flow
branches.waitBefore: SLA: replied-to within 24 hours, and same day if the reply lands before 18:00 IST. Weekend replies answered Monday by 11:00. Never auto-acknowledge; an autoresponder on a peer-to-peer clinical email destroys exactly the thing this stage is buying.

branches.signal: Replied with a decline, or asks to be removed
branches.measuredHow: Same inbox. Route to POST /api/suppressions/add?email= only for an explicit removal request; a decline for this edition is not a decline forever and goes to a 'next edition' list instead.
branches.goesTo: Suppression, or the next-edition list
branches.waitBefore: Removal requests actioned within 24 hours regardless of wording. Treat any negative reply as an unsubscribe in intent even when it is not phrased as one.

branches.signal: Replied asking to speak, present, or partner
branches.measuredHow: Same inbox, flagged by hand. This is the outcome the flow exists for beyond registrations.
branches.goesTo: Founder or partnerships owner, same day
branches.waitBefore: Under 4 hours during working hours. A faculty or partnership reply that waits overnight is a lost one.

branches.signal: Opened but did not reply or register
branches.measuredHow: tracking_event OPEN/HUMAN for the stage 4 campaign minus the reply log and the Zoom registrant export.
branches.goesTo: Stage 6a last chance
branches.waitBefore: 96 hours.

stages.successMetric: 40-50% HUMAN open, because a short plain-text email from a named human on a personal-inbox list outperforms every designed template in the flow. Reply rate 3-6%, which is 15-27 real conversations. Registrations attributable to this stage 25-45. On this list a reply converts at roughly ten times the rate of a click, so 20 replies handled well is worth more than 200 extra opens. Median reply latency is the metric to publish internally: under 6 working hours is good, over 24 means the stage should not run next time.
stages.killCriteria: Do not send this stage if fewer than two people can hold the 24-hour SLA that week. An email that invites a reply and then does not answer it is worse than never asking, and on a clinician list it is remembered. Do not automate any part of the response. Do not send the peer-to-peer cut from anyone who is not actually a clinician; the claimed 3-5x lift comes from the sender being a peer, and a non-clinician sending it is a misrepresentation. Do not send to anyone with an open unanswered reply from an earlier stage.
stages.teachingNote: Replies are the only signal in this entire flow that the platform cannot measure at all, and they are simultaneously the most valuable one. That is the lesson: instrument what you can, but do not let the instrumentation decide what matters. Build the human loop first, then close the gap in code. VERP is the cheap fix here, roughly a one-line change to a Reply-To slot that is already per-message, plus a scanner and a credential that is not trapped in someone's browser session.

stages.name: The Two Failure Modes (objection answer, and one retry)
stages.purpose: Stop treating 'did not register' as one problem. Someone who opened and did not click has an objection; someone who never opened has a delivery or attention problem. They need different emails, and the second group needs exactly one more attempt, ever.
stages.timing: 5a at T-7, Sat 19 Sep 2026, 11:00 IST, the same unhurried Saturday slot that worked for the give, because answering an objection needs a body someone will actually read. 5b at T-5, Mon 21 Sep 2026, 21:15 IST, deliberately the opposite end of the day from the original 07:10 send, because a time-of-day change is the highest-yield variable available for recovering non-openers.
stages.audience: 5a: Stage 3 openers who did not click, approximately 430. 5b: no HUMAN open on Stage 2 or Stage 3, approximately 2,300, minus anyone with a silence counter of 3 or more from previous editions.
stages.entryCondition: Non-registrant as of the morning of the send, not suppressed, and not already in a reply conversation.
stages.exitCondition: Registered, replied, or continues to Stage 6a (5a) or straight to the Stage 8 pool (5b non-openers).

branches.signal: 5a: clicked the agenda or faculty link
branches.measuredHow: tracking_event CLICK/HUMAN for the 5a campaign. Give the agenda PDF, faculty bios and registration form three distinct URLs, since GET /api/analytics/links groups by destination string and cannot separate two buttons pointing at the same place.
branches.goesTo: Stage 6a with the shortest, most urgent copy cut
branches.waitBefore: 72 hours.

branches.measuredHow: tracking_event OPEN/HUMAN for the 5b campaign. Because the first send produced nothing, this is a clean recovery measurement: the retry rate divided by the original cohort is your inbox-placement health indicator for the cold segment.
branches.goesTo: Stage 6a
branches.waitBefore: 72 hours, closing Wed 23 Sep before dawn so 6a can cut its list.

branches.measuredHow: The 5b recipient export minus its HUMAN open set. Silence counter reaches 4. This is now four consecutive sends with zero verified human engagement.
branches.goesTo: Removed from Stage 6a entirely and placed in the Stage 8 sunset pool
branches.waitBefore: 72 hours.

branches.signal: Bounce or complaint spike on the retry
branches.measuredHow: GET /api/analytics/summary?campaignId=<5b>&days=1 for complaintRate and bounceRate, cross-checked against GET /api/suppressions. Complaints concentrate on retries to non-openers more than on any other send type.
branches.goesTo: Immediate halt of remaining sends to the cold segment
branches.waitBefore: 24 hours, and check before Stage 6a is scheduled.

stages.successMetric: 5a: 30-38% open (this cohort already proved it opens) and 6-9% click, since the whole email is the objection answer. 5b: 8-12% HUMAN open, which is roughly half to two-thirds of what the first email achieved on the same people; anything above 12% means your first send's timing was wrong, not your list. Combined registrations 20-35. Complaint rate on 5b under 0.08% is the pass condition, and it matters more than the registrations.
stages.killCriteria: Never send more than one retry to a non-opener. Ever. Anyone at a silence counter of 3 or more entering this stage skips 5b and goes directly to Stage 8. Do not send 5b if Stage 3's cold cut showed a complaint rate above 0.08%. Do not send 5a with the same subject line as Stage 3; if the objection email looks like the ask email, the opener who ignored the ask will ignore it identically. Skip both if the contact has had three emails in the previous seven days, which on this calendar means checking the cold cohort carefully.
stages.teachingNote: Non-response is not one behaviour. Aggregating the objection-holders and the never-saw-its into a single 'unconverted' bucket and sending them the same reminder is the most common structural error in webinar marketing, and it simultaneously under-serves the people who are close and over-mails the people who are gone. The one-retry rule is a reputation rule, not a copy rule: repeatedly mailing verified non-openers is the fastest route to a Gmail bulk-sender problem on an 88% freemail list.

stages.name: Close and Convert (last chance for non-registrants, join track for registrants)
stages.purpose: Harvest the deadline-driven registrations, and separately, protect the attendance rate by making sure every registrant actually shows up. These are two completely different jobs and must never share an email.
stages.timing: 6a last chance at T-3, Wed 23 Sep 2026, 07:10 IST, with a real close at Fri 25 Sep 18:00 IST. 6b registrant-only at T-2, Thu 24 Sep 2026, 21:15 IST, when someone can actually put the calendar hold in. Event day Sat 26 Sep: 09:00 IST Zoom link reminder and 18:00 IST T-90-minute nudge, both registrants only. The 09:00 slot exists because Saturday morning is when weekend plans get fixed; 18:00 exists because free-webinar no-show is overwhelmingly a forgetting problem, not an intent problem.
stages.audience: 6a: all remaining non-registrants with at least one HUMAN open anywhere in the flow, approximately 1,450. Explicitly excludes the four-times-silent, who are already in the Stage 8 pool. 6b and the day-of sends: registrants only, approximately 280-350 by then.
stages.entryCondition: 6a: unregistered, at least one HUMAN open in tracking_event across any flow campaign, not suppressed. 6b: present in the Zoom registrant export pulled at 09:00 that morning.
stages.exitCondition: Registration closes Fri 25 Sep 18:00 IST for 6a. 6b exits when the event starts.

branches.measuredHow: Zoom registrant export delta between Wed 23 Sep 09:00 and Fri 25 Sep 18:00, cross-referenced against tracking_event CLICK/HUMAN on the registration URL for the 6a campaign.
branches.goesTo: Registrant track, receives the day-of sends only (they miss 6b, which is fine, the day-of email carries the join instructions)
branches.waitBefore: Pull the export twice daily through the close window. The cost of mailing a fresh registrant a last-chance email is disproportionate to the effort of avoiding it.

branches.measuredHow: Zoom attendee log CSV, the same export format as attendeelog_2026_06_27. Join and leave times give dwell; the Horizon I benchmark of 80+ minutes average watch is the bar.
branches.goesTo: Stage 7a
branches.waitBefore: Export within 2 hours of the event ending, so Stage 7a can send at E+1 10:00.

branches.measuredHow: Zoom registrant export minus attendee log. Note both are Zoom artefacts, not JCF-Mailer ones: the platform has no conversion or attendance concept at all, and GET /api/mailer/success is a static page that records nothing.
branches.goesTo: Stage 7b
branches.waitBefore: Same 2-hour window.

branches.signal: Did not register by the close
branches.measuredHow: Full flow recipient set minus the final registrant export.
branches.goesTo: Stage 7c if they have any HUMAN engagement, Stage 8 if they have none
branches.waitBefore: Wait until after the event. A non-registrant who is sent the recording at E+3 converts for the next edition; one who is sent another ask at E+0 does not.

stages.successMetric: 6a: 15-20% open, 2-3% click, 60-100 registrations. Last chance is reliably the second-largest registration driver in a flow like this after the first ask, which is why it earns its slot despite being the most fatiguing send. 6b: 55-70% open, and its real metric is downstream. Day-of 09:00 email 50-65% open, 18:00 nudge 45-60%. Attendance target 35-45% of registrants, so 280-350 registrants should produce 100-155 live. Whole-flow target: 220-300 list-attributable registrations against a roughly 163 baseline from the two-email approach, plus whatever off-list channels contribute.
stages.killCriteria: Never send the Zoom join link to a non-registrant, at any stage, for any reason. It is the one hard rule of the flow and it exists both for capacity and because it is the only thing that makes registration feel worth doing. Do not send 6a to anyone with zero HUMAN opens across the whole flow; the marginal registration is not worth the complaint. Do not use a fake deadline: if registration will in fact stay open, say something else. Do not send the 18:00 nudge if the event is cancelled or the faculty has dropped, and have a substitute email drafted for that case before the day.
stages.teachingNote: Registrants and non-registrants are opposite problems from T-3 onward: one needs persuading, the other needs reminding, and an email that tries to do both does neither. Note also that this stage is where the platform's missing send-window control bites hardest. There are no quiet hours, no recipient timezone and no per-campaign pacing, so the only thing standing between your list and a 03:00 IST blast is the human typing the value into POST /api/campaigns/schedule?when=. Write the send times into the runbook, not into someone's memory.

stages.name: Post-Event Three-Way Fork
stages.purpose: Turn one event into the next event's warm list, by treating attendees, registered-no-shows and engaged-never-registered as three different relationships with three different next steps.
stages.timing: 7a and 7b at E+1, Sun 27 Sep 2026, 10:00 and 10:30 IST. Sunday morning while the session is still fresh, and because the certificate is the single highest-click asset in the entire flow and deserves a clean slot. 7c at E+3, Tue 29 Sep 2026, 07:10 IST, deliberately two days later so the recording arrives as proof of what happened rather than as a consolation prize sent in the same breath.
stages.audience: 7a attendees, from the Zoom attendee log, roughly 100-155. 7b registered-no-shows, roughly 150-200. 7c engaged never-registered (at least one HUMAN open, no registration), roughly 900-1,200.
stages.entryCondition: Membership determined entirely by the two Zoom exports pulled within 2 hours of the event ending, cross-matched to subscriber emails.
stages.exitCondition: Sent. 7a and 7b members are promoted into the seed cohorts for the next edition's Stage 1. 7c members with no click here fall into the Stage 8 pool.

branches.measuredHow: tracking_event CLICK/HUMAN on the certificate URL for the 7a campaign. Keep the certificate, recording and slides on three distinct URLs so GET /api/analytics/links can separate them.
branches.goesTo: Next edition's C1 cohort, the warmest list JCF has
branches.waitBefore: 7 days. Certificate clicks have a long tail; people fetch them when they need them for CME records, not when the email arrives.

branches.measuredHow: Monitored replyTo inbox, GET /api/mail/messages. The email asks one direct question, which is what generates the replies.
branches.goesTo: Human, within 24 hours, and into the faculty and topic pipeline
branches.waitBefore: Zero. Same SLA as Stage 4.

branches.measuredHow: tracking_event CLICK/HUMAN on the recording URL for the 7b campaign, cross-checked against the 7a set to confirm the fork was cut correctly.
branches.goesTo: Next edition's C2 cohort, treated as intent-proven but attendance-blocked, which changes the next Stage 1 copy from persuasion to logistics
branches.waitBefore: 7 days.

branches.signal: 7c: clicked the recording or the save-the-date
branches.measuredHow: tracking_event CLICK/HUMAN for the 7c campaign, split by URL.
branches.goesTo: Next edition's C3 cohort
branches.waitBefore: 7 days.

branches.measuredHow: 7c recipient export minus its HUMAN open set. Silence counter reaches 5 for the cold cohort members.
branches.goesTo: Stage 8 sunset pool
branches.waitBefore: 7 days.

stages.successMetric: 7a: 55-70% open, and certificate click 70-85% of openers, the highest click rate anywhere in the flow. Reply rate 4-8%, which is where next edition's topics and sometimes next edition's faculty come from. 7b: 35-45% open, 25-35% recording click, and no unsubscribe spike, which is the test of whether the copy was genuinely guilt-free. 7c: 15-20% open, 2-4% click. The composite metric that matters: next edition's C1 plus C2 seed should be at least 250 addresses, versus the roughly 400 available today from the June event.
stages.killCriteria: Do not send 7a until certificates actually exist and one has been downloaded end to end by a human. Promising a certificate and delivering a broken link to the people who just gave you two hours is the most expensive small failure in this flow. Do not send 7b any variant of 'we missed you' or 'sorry you could not make it': a no-show on a free Saturday-evening webinar is usually a clinical emergency, and the guilt framing is both wrong and counterproductive. Do not send 7c if the recording is not publicly accessible without a login. Skip 7c entirely for anyone in the Stage 8 pool with a silence counter of 4 or more.
stages.teachingNote: Most webinar campaigns end at the event, which throws away the only moment when the audience has actual evidence of quality. An attendee is a testimonial, a co-chair suggestion and a next-edition seat; a no-show is a logistics problem, not a rejection; a never-registered opener has now watched other people find it worthwhile. Three completely different next sentences. The post-event fork is where a one-off webinar becomes a series, and it is the single stage most responsible for the next campaign starting warm instead of cold.

stages.name: Graceful Sunset
stages.purpose: Remove the permanently silent from the active list in a way that protects domain reputation for the next edition, without permanently burning addresses that might simply have been mis-timed.
stages.timing: 8a at E+9, Mon 5 Oct 2026, 21:15 IST. Nine days after the event so it does not collide with the post-event mail, and evening because a 'should we stop emailing you' question reads better as a quiet one. 8b is not a send: it is executed at E+16, Mon 12 Oct 2026, seven days after 8a, which is the full window a HUMAN open needs on this audience.
stages.audience: Zero HUMAN opens across every campaign in the flow, silence counter of 4 or more, approximately 1,600-1,900. Excludes anyone added to the list within the previous 21 days and anyone who replied at any point.
stages.entryCondition: No row in tracking_event with classification='HUMAN' for any campaign in this flow, for that subscriber, after POST /api/analytics/reclassify has been run over the full history.
stages.exitCondition: Clicked 'keep me' and stays on the active list, or is moved to Horizon-Dormant-2026 at 8b.

branches.measuredHow: tracking_event CLICK/HUMAN on the keep-me URL for the 8a campaign. Two distinct URLs are mandatory here so GET /api/analytics/links can tell keep from remove; they cannot be the same destination with different anchor text.
branches.goesTo: Stays active, silence counter reset to 0, and is worth more than most of the list because they have now explicitly opted back in
branches.waitBefore: 7 days. Shorter windows sunset people who were simply on leave, which on a clinician list is common.

branches.measuredHow: The remove URL should be {{UNSUBSCRIBE_LINK}} itself, so the click writes global_suppression with reason UNSUBSCRIBED through the existing TrackingController path and needs no manual step. Verify via GET /api/suppressions.
branches.goesTo: Global suppression, permanently, automatically
branches.waitBefore: Immediate.

branches.measuredHow: 8a recipient export (GET /api/campaigns/{id}/export?status=SENT) minus its HUMAN open and click sets.
branches.goesTo: Horizon-Dormant-2026 via POST /api/subscribers/remove-from-list then POST /api/subscribers/add-to-list. Not suppressed.
branches.waitBefore: 7 days, hard.

branches.measuredHow: The no-response set intersected with verification_result.verdict IN ('RISKY') or catchAll = true. These are the addresses that are both dead weight and a reputation liability.
branches.goesTo: POST /api/suppressions/add?email=, permanent global suppression
branches.waitBefore: 7 days, and only for the intersection, never for silence alone.

stages.successMetric: 6-10% HUMAN open on the sunset email, which will be the lowest in the flow by design. Keep-me click 1.5-3.0%, so 30-55 people saved and re-consented. If the keep-me rate comes in above 3%, your sunset threshold was too aggressive and you should require five silent sends next time rather than four. The real success metric is the next edition's Stage 1d cold-cohort numbers: an active list trimmed from roughly 3,363 to roughly 1,600 should show HUMAN open rise from 12-18% into the 20-26% band and bounce fall below 1%, which is what buys inbox placement for every future send.
stages.killCriteria: Do not send to anyone added in the last 21 days; they have not had a fair chance. Do not send to anyone who ever replied, even if they never opened a tracked pixel, because image blocking makes open data silently wrong for a slice of this audience and a reply is proof of life that outranks it. Do not use global suppression as the default exit: global_suppression has email as its primary key and is enforced at three separate points in the send path, so it is effectively irreversible and it would block a future consented re-subscribe. List removal is the reversible action and should be the default. Do not run this stage at all if POST /api/analytics/reclassify has not been run first, because the classifier is what separates a genuine non-opener from an Apple MPP user whose real opens were never attributed.
stages.teachingNote: Sunsetting feels like losing 1,700 contacts. It is actually buying inbox placement for the 1,600 who remain, and on an 88% Gmail-and-Yahoo list that is the difference between the next edition's first email landing in Primary or in Promotions. Two disciplines make it safe: give people a real choice before you act on their silence, and prefer the reversible removal over the irreversible suppression. The number to publish to the team is not list size, it is engaged list size, and this stage is the only one in the flow that improves it.

tests.stage: Programme-wide carve-out, applied before Stage 1 (T-21) and held for all 6 stages
tests.hypothesis: Because 35 of the 163 June registrants came from off-list channels (Zoom snapshot vs users.csv join), we believe a no-mail holdout will reveal that a meaningful share of registrations would have happened anyway, measured by registration rate in the holdout vs the mailed group joined on email from the Zoom registrant export.
tests.variantA: Mailed: receives all 6 Horizon IV stages (n approx 3,023).
tests.variantB: Holdout: receives zero campaign email for this edition; still reachable via social, WhatsApp and word of mouth (n = 340).
tests.primaryMetric: Registration rate by event day (Zoom registrant export joined on lowercased email to the arm assignment CSV).
tests.guardrailMetric: None on the holdout itself. The cost side: 340 unmailed people at an expected 6% registration is approximately 20 registrations foregone. Track it explicitly so the trade is visible.
tests.sampleSizeMath: Verified roster: horizon-clean.csv = 3,363 data rows, 3,363 unique emails, 12 blank first names, 167 domains, 92.1% free-mail (recomputed from the file, not quoted). Hash holdout at 10% gives exactly 340 / 3,023. Formula: n/arm = 7.849 x [p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)] / (p2-p1)^2 where 7.849 = (1.96 + 0.8416)^2 (two-sided alpha 0.05, 80% power). Assume organic registration among never-mailed p1 = 1.0% and mailed p2 = 5.0%: 7.849 x (0.0099 + 0.0475) / 0.0016 = 282 per arm at equal allocation. This is a 9:1 unequal split, so the smaller arm needs n_small = n_equal x (1 + 1/9) / 2 = 282 x 0.556 = 157. We have 340 in the holdout, more than double. VERDICT FITS. If the true mailed rate is only 3% rather than 5%, required n_small rises to roughly 470 and the test fails, so this is powered only for the case where email is doing most of the work.
tests.decisionRule: Read once, 48h after the event, never before. Two-proportion z-test on registration rate. If mailed - holdout lift is significant at p<0.05, record the absolute incremental registration count and use it as the denominator for every future 'this campaign produced X registrations' claim. If p>=0.05, do NOT conclude email does not work: state 'holdout n=340 cannot resolve a lift below 4 percentage points' and roll the holdout forward unchanged into Horizon V so the two editions pool to n_small=680. Keep the same holdout people across editions (same salt) so the pooled read stays clean.

tests.stage: Stage 1 (T-21, Save the Date) and Stage 2 (T-14, Registration Open) - persistent frame across both, then frozen
tests.hypothesis: Because the June sends went out from partnership@jarurat.care with ambiguous authorship (script says partnership@, drafted copy signs as Priyanka, the older drip signs as Ubhay Anand) and because a 92.1% free-mail personal-inbox doctor list treats organisational mail as bulk, we believe a named human sender identity will cause a higher unique human open rate than an organisational one, measured by reliableOpens/delivered from GET /api/analytics/summary per arm campaign.
tests.variantA: fromName = 'Jarurat Care Foundation', replyTo = partnership@jarurat.care, sign-off 'Jarurat Care Foundation'.
tests.variantB: fromName = 'Priyanka Joshi | Jarurat Care Foundation', replyTo = priyanka@jarurat.care, sign-off 'Priyanka Joshi, Founder, Jarurat Care Foundation'.
tests.primaryMetric: Unique HUMAN open rate = reliableOpens / delivered, from the classified analytics stack only (GET /api/analytics/summary?campaignId=). Never GET /api/campaigns, which reports the inflated legacy openedAt rate.
tests.guardrailMetric: Complaint rate must stay below 0.100% and bounce rate below 2.00% in BOTH arms (AnalyticsService complaintDangerLine 0.1 / bounceDangerLine 2.0). Secondary guardrail: unsubscribe rate per arm must not exceed the other arm by more than 0.30pt.
tests.sampleSizeMath: Available: 3,363 roster - 340 holdout = 3,023 mailed. First send on a new domain (horizonevent.info) to a list last touched in June via Postmark, 92.1% free-mail: assume 6% undeliverable, so delivered approx 2,842, i.e. 1,421 per arm. Actual SHA-256 mod 2 split on the real file gave 1,744 / 1,619 pre-bounce; the harmonic effective n is 1,679 vs 1,681 for a perfect split, so the imbalance costs under 0.2% of power and is not worth fixing. Required: at p1 = 0.30, p2 = 0.35 (5pt MDE), n/arm = 7.849 x (0.2100 + 0.2275) / 0.0025 = 1,374. Need 2,748 delivered, have 2,842. FITS with 3% headroom. At the pessimistic baseline p1 = 0.25 -> 0.30 the requirement drops to 1,248/arm; at p1 = 0.35 -> 0.40 it rises to 1,468/arm and the test becomes marginal. Achieved MDE at 1,421/arm, base 30% = 4.9pt (30.0% -> 34.9%, +16% relative). Sender identity is the one lever in this programme where a 5pt effect is genuinely plausible, which is why it gets the whole list and the first two stages.
tests.decisionRule: Single pre-registered read at 72h after the Stage 2 send, pooling Stage 1 + Stage 2 at PERSON level (opened at least one of the two stages), not at email level, because two observations on the same person are not two samples. Declare a winner only if all three hold: p<0.05 on the two-proportion z-test, absolute difference >= 4.9pt, and complaint rate <0.100% in both arms. On a win, apply the winning fromName/replyTo to every campaign from Stage 3 onward and record it as the new default. On p>=0.05, declare NO WINNER out loud, default to the named-human arm (it is also the cheaper reply path since replies land in a real mailbox), log the observed difference with its 95% CI, and re-run identically in Horizon V so the two editions pool to 2,842/arm and the MDE falls to 3.5pt. No peeking at 24h.

tests.stage: Stage 2 (T-14, Registration Open + faculty) - crossed 2x2 with HZN-T1 using an independent salt
tests.hypothesis: Because the list is an untagged mix of consultants, fellows, residents and students and the brief bans 'Dear Doctor' generic framing, we believe a subject naming the specific clinical controversy will cause a higher open rate than one naming the faculty brand, measured by reliableOpens/delivered.
tests.variantA: Faculty-authority framing: 'Dr Milind Javle and Dr Manish Shah on gastric and GE junction cancer | Horizon Series, 27 Sept'.
tests.variantB: Clinical-specificity framing: 'Perioperative IO and MATTERHORN: what actually changes in your Monday clinic'.
tests.primaryMetric: Unique HUMAN open rate (reliableOpens / delivered) on the Stage 2 campaigns, main effect collapsed across the two HZN-T1 sender arms.
tests.guardrailMetric: Complaint rate <0.100% per arm; unsubscribe rate per arm; and click-to-open rate must not fall more than 3pt in the winning arm (a subject that wins opens by over-promising and then loses CTOR is a loss, not a win).
tests.sampleSizeMath: Same denominator as HZN-T1: approx 2,842 delivered, and because HZN-T2 uses an independent salt it is orthogonal to the sender split, so the subject main effect is estimated on 1,421 per LEVEL even though the stage runs as four campaigns of roughly 710 each (verified on the real file: the S1 x S2 cross-tab came out 846 / 898 / 835 / 784). Required at p1 = 0.30 -> 0.35: 1,374/arm. Nominally FITS. But this is the test the Apple MPP problem eats. If a fraction m of true openers are only ever seen as APPLE_MPP and therefore excluded from reliableOpens, both the measured rate and the measured difference shrink by (1-m). At m = 0.25 a TRUE 5pt lift shows up as a measured 3.75pt lift on a measured baseline of 22.5%, which needs 7.849 x (0.1744 + 0.1936) / 0.001406 = 2,054 per arm = 4,108 delivered. We have 2,842. Under 25% MPP this test is UNDERPOWERED for the very effect it is designed to find, and m is unknown until the first send reports mppOpens.
tests.decisionRule: Do not pre-register this as confirmatory. Read GET /api/analytics/classifier first and compute m = mppOpens / (reliableOpens + mppOpens). If m < 0.15, treat as confirmatory: winner requires p<0.05 and >= 4.9pt. If m >= 0.15, the open metric is not trustworthy at this n: switch the primary to click rate on the registration link (base approx 3%, CI on a difference is +/-1.26pt at this n, so a 2pt click gap IS readable), report the open difference as directional only with its CI, and never write the word 'winner'. Either way, carry the losing subject family forward as the Stage 4 subject so the same contrast is measured a second time, and pool across Horizon IV, V and VI before making any permanent copy rule.

tests.stage: Stage 3 (T-9, Academic value) - crossed 2x2 with HZN-T4
tests.hypothesis: Because the entire list is effectively single-timezone Indian clinicians on personal free-mail accounts and the June Postmark run had no send-window logic at all, we believe a post-clinic evening send will cause a higher open rate than a mid-morning send, measured by reliableOpens/delivered on two campaigns scheduled 9 hours apart on the same day.
tests.primaryMetric: Unique HUMAN open rate within 48h of send (use GET /api/analytics/series to hold the window constant at 48h for both arms, otherwise the morning arm gets 9 extra hours of exposure and the comparison is rigged).
tests.guardrailMetric: Complaint rate <0.100% per arm. Operational guardrail: SesSender.awaitSendSlot is process-wide at 12/s shared with transactional mail, so schedule the two arms on different scheduledAt minutes by design here, and confirm neither blast overlaps a transactional burst.
tests.sampleSizeMath: Mailable at Stage 3 after Stage 1-2 bounces and unsubs: approx 2,800 delivered, 1,400 per arm. Achieved MDE at 1,400/arm, base 30% = 4.95pt. The problem is not the arithmetic, it is the effect size. Published send-hour effects on a single-timezone list are 1 to 3 percentage points. Detecting 2pt at base 30% requires 7.849 x (0.2100 + 0.2176) / 0.0004 = 8,390 per arm = 16,780 delivered, which is 5.0x the entire roster. Detecting 3pt requires 3,760 per arm = 7,520 delivered, 2.2x the roster. This test cannot be won on this list in this edition, or in any single edition.
tests.decisionRule: Run it anyway because it is free to run, but pre-register it as EXPLORATORY with no significance claim. Fix the rule now: alternate 11:00 and 20:00 across all six stages of Horizon IV, V and VI using the same persistent hash arms, log open rate per arm per stage, and only after 6 stages x 3 editions (pooled 8,400 person-stages per arm, still only 1,400 distinct people per arm) look at the direction. If both editions point the same way by more than 2pt, adopt that hour as the house default by fiat and stop testing it. Explicitly forbidden: declaring 20:00 the winner off one stage with a 2pt gap, whose 95% CI is +/-3.39pt and therefore includes zero.

tests.stage: Stage 3 (T-9, Academic value) - crossed 2x2 with HZN-T3
tests.hypothesis: Because the strategy brief argues the AI-drafted timeline copy 'missed everything that actually drives conversion' and prescribes shorter warmer plain-style notes, while the audience brief demands a layered value stack (senior hook in the first two lines, resident hook mid, student hook last), we believe a short note will cause a higher click rate than a long layered one, measured by reliableClicks/delivered on the registration link.
tests.variantA: Long: approx 220 words, layered value stack, full agenda summary, faculty affiliations, certificate and recording promise.
tests.variantB: Short: approx 90 words, one clinical question, one line of proof, one link. No agenda block.
tests.primaryMetric: Unique HUMAN click rate on the registration URL (reliableClicks / delivered, cross-checked against GET /api/analytics/links, which groups by destination URL only, so each arm MUST use a distinct UTM-tagged registration URL or the arms are indistinguishable in the link report).
tests.guardrailMetric: Unsubscribe rate per arm (the long arm is the plausible unsub risk) and complaint rate <0.100%. Also watch Gmail 102KB clipping: run POST /api/campaignsplus/templates/validate on the long arm before send.
tests.sampleSizeMath: 1,400 per level at Stage 3 (main effect across the T3 time split). Click baseline for non-profit healthcare is 2-4%; take 3%. Required to detect 3% -> 4% (1pt, +33% relative): 7.849 x (0.0291 + 0.0384) / 0.0001 = 5,298 per arm = 10,596 delivered, 3.2x the roster. To detect 3% -> 4.5% (+50% relative): 2,514 per arm = 5,028 delivered, 1.5x the roster. Achieved MDE at 1,400/arm on a 3% base = 2.08pt, i.e. the effect must be 3% -> 5.1% (+69%) to reach significance. Email length does not move clicks by 69%. FAILS on power by roughly 2 to 4x.
tests.decisionRule: Exploratory only. Read click rate, click-to-open rate and unsubscribe rate per arm with 95% CIs and publish all three with the CI, never the point estimate alone. Pre-registered action: if the short arm's unsub rate is lower by any amount and its click rate is not lower by more than 0.5pt, adopt short as the house style for Stages 1-3 on operational grounds (cheaper to write, lower clip risk) and stop testing length. This is a decision made on cost and risk, not on a significance claim, and it should be written down that way.

tests.stage: Stage 4 (T-4, Final reminder) - crossed 2x2 with HZN-T8
tests.hypothesis: Because the June copy shipped a bare 'Registration Link: [Insert Registration Link]' placeholder CTA and the platform rewrites every href for tracking anyway, we believe a single high-contrast button will cause a higher click rate than a plain inline text link on a doctor audience reading mostly on mobile Gmail, measured by reliableClicks/delivered.
tests.variantA: Plain inline text link inside the sentence, plus the bare URL on its own line beneath it.
tests.variantB: Single centred button, 44px tall, one colour, plus a plain fallback URL line beneath it.
tests.primaryMetric: Unique HUMAN click rate on the registration link. Distinct UTM per arm is mandatory: per-link attribution is by destination URL string with no link IDs, so two CTAs pointing at the same URL are literally the same row in GET /api/analytics/links.
tests.guardrailMetric: Complaint rate <0.100%; and the BOT/PROXY click share per arm from GET /api/analytics/classifier, because a big button is more likely to be fetched by a security scanner and inflate the arm artificially. If bot click share differs between arms by more than 3pt, the comparison is void.
tests.sampleSizeMath: Stage 4 mailable approx 2,780, so 1,390 per level for the main effect (four campaigns of approx 695 each). Click baseline 3%. Required for 3% -> 4%: 5,298 per arm. Required for 3% -> 6% (a doubling, the only effect this n can see): 7.849 x (0.0291 + 0.0564) / 0.0009 = 746 per arm, which we DO have. So the honest framing is: this test is powered to detect a doubling of click rate and nothing less. Achieved MDE at 1,390/arm on a 3% base = 2.09pt (3.0% -> 5.1%). A button-vs-link effect of that size has never been observed anywhere. The 95% CI on the click difference at this n is +/-1.26pt, so a 0.4pt gap, which is what you will actually see, is noise.
tests.decisionRule: Exploratory. Pre-registered rule: ship the button in both arms of Horizon V regardless of the Horizon IV result unless the plain-link arm beat it by more than 1.3pt (the CI half-width). Rationale stated in advance: accessibility and mobile tap target are design decisions that do not need a p-value, and burning a test cell on them across six editions is a worse use of the list than testing proof framing. Record the number, move on.

tests.stage: Stage 4 (T-4) - sent only to the not-yet-registered slice
tests.hypothesis: Because the strategy brief's strongest claimed tactic is peer-to-peer contact and because a reply is a far stronger commitment signal than a click, we believe a reply-request CTA ('reply with the word AGENDA and I will send the full programme') will cause more registrations among non-registrants than a link CTA, measured by registrations attributed offline via the Zoom export.
tests.variantA: Link CTA: 'Register here' with the tracked registration URL.
tests.variantB: Reply CTA: no link in the body, 'reply with AGENDA and I will send you the programme and the Zoom link', reply-to set to a monitored human mailbox.
tests.primaryMetric: Registration rate by event day, joined offline from the Zoom registrant export. Reply count is NOT available as a metric.
tests.guardrailMetric: Complaint rate <0.100%. Real operational guardrail: a reply-request generates inbound volume that a two-person team must actually answer within 24h, or the tactic converts worse than doing nothing.
tests.sampleSizeMath: The audience is non-registrants only. Extrapolating the June ratio (128 of 3,367 emailed were already registered at send time, 3.8%), by T-4 in a properly run 4-stage sequence expect 6-10% registered, so the non-registrant pool is approximately 2,550, i.e. 1,275 per arm. Registration base among people who have already ignored three emails is low, call it 2%. Required to detect 2% -> 5%: 7.849 x (0.0196 + 0.0475) / 0.0009 = 585 per arm, which FITS. So the arithmetic is not the blocker here. The blocker is capability 7: there is no reply detection anywhere. CampaignRecipient has no REPLIED state, no In-Reply-To capture, no VERP, and MailboxAccess keeps the mailbox secret in a browser HttpSession so no background job can read the inbox. Replies would have to be counted by a human reading a mailbox and tallying by hand, with no link back to arm assignment except by matching the sender address to the arm CSV.
tests.decisionRule: Do not run as an A/B test in Horizon IV. Instead fund the VERP build listed in the audit (per-recipient Reply-To of the form reply+{token}@jarurat.care set in SesSender.build, campaign_reply table, ReplyScanner on a 5-minute schedule with a credential from an env var rather than a browser session). That is a medium build and it is the single highest-value platform gap for this audience, because reply rate is the metric that actually predicts webinar attendance for clinicians. Re-open this test in Horizon V once replies are machine-countable. In the meantime, run the reply CTA UNTESTED to the whole non-registrant slice at Stage 4, since the brief already believes in it and an untested tactic beats a test you cannot measure.

tests.hypothesis: Because merge depth is capped at three tokens and 12 of 3,363 rows have a blank first name, we believe first-name greeting personalisation will cause a higher click rate on the day-of Zoom link than a neutral collegial greeting, measured by reliableClicks/delivered.
tests.variantA: Neutral: 'Dear Colleague,' with no merge tokens anywhere in the body.
tests.variantB: Personalised: '{{FIRST_NAME}},' greeting with honorific handling (CampaignService.java:417-428 renders 'Dr. Akanksha Chichra' as 'Dr. Akanksha') plus one mid-body '{{FIRST_NAME}}, the session opens at 7:30' reprise.
tests.primaryMetric: Unique HUMAN click rate on the join link.
tests.guardrailMetric: Zero broken greetings. Hard pre-send check: the 12 blank-first-name rows must be excluded from the personalised arm entirely, because applyMergeFields blanks unresolved tokens and would render 'Dear ,'. Also complaint rate <0.100%.
tests.sampleSizeMath: Day-of audience approx 2,760 mailable, 1,380 per arm. Day-of click base is higher, call it 6%. Achieved MDE at 1,380/arm on a 6% base = 2.79pt (6.0% -> 8.8%, +46% relative). Required to detect a realistic personalisation effect of 6% -> 7% (1pt): 7.849 x (0.0564 + 0.0651) / 0.0001 = 9,536 per arm = 19,072 delivered, 5.7x the roster. FAILS by a factor of about 6. Note also the structural limit that kills the interesting version of this test: campaign subjects are passed to SES raw with no merge pass (CampaignService.sendOne:201), so first-name-in-subject, the personalisation variant with the largest documented effect, CANNOT be tested at all without a code change.
tests.decisionRule: Exploratory, and honestly closer to a QA exercise than a test. Pre-registered action independent of result: keep {{FIRST_NAME}} personalisation on permanently, because the brief already bans 'Dear Doctor' generic address and the cost is zero. Use the test purely to confirm the honorific renderer behaves on a real send and that no blank greeting shipped. If the team wants the real personalisation test, fund the one-line change that runs campaign subjects through applyMergeFields, then test first-name-in-subject in Horizon V where the effect is large enough to be visible at 1,400/arm.

tests.stage: Stage 4 (T-4, Final reminder) - crossed 2x2 with HZN-T5, and repeated at Stage 3 of Horizon V and VI
tests.hypothesis: Because JCF has two genuinely different and both-defensible proof stories, we believe event social proof will cause more registrations from a clinician audience than mission framing, measured by registration rate joined from the Zoom export.
tests.variantA: Social proof: '309 clinicians joined the June gastric session. Faculty from MD Anderson, Weill Cornell, Roswell Park and Princess Margaret. 80+ minute average watch time, 55% international audience.'
tests.variantB: Mission framing: 'Bridging international research with Indian clinical realities. Across 300 families we have measured, financial toxicity sits at 4.42 out of 10. This forum exists to close that gap.'
tests.primaryMetric: Cumulative registration rate by event day (Zoom export joined on email to arm assignment), with unique HUMAN click rate as the fast-read proxy.
tests.guardrailMetric: Complaint rate <0.100% and unsubscribe rate per arm. Reputational guardrail: every number in arm A must be traceable to the attendee log or the Horizon deck, and every number in arm B to the founders-office deck. Do not use the 96% cost-reduction figure, which the deck itself footnotes as an estimate, and do not use the stale '200+ patients' from the March knowledge base when the live figure is 670.
tests.sampleSizeMath: 1,390 per level at Stage 4. Cumulative registration base by T-4, call it 6%. Required to detect 6% -> 8% (2pt, +33% relative): 7.849 x (0.0564 + 0.0736) / 0.0004 = 2,551 per arm = 5,102 delivered, 1.5x the roster. Required for 6% -> 7%: 9,536 per arm. Achieved MDE at 1,390/arm = 2.79pt. FAILS in a single edition by about 1.8x. BUT this is the one underpowered test worth running to schedule: because the same two frames can be repeated across editions with the SAME persistent hash arms, three editions pool to approximately 4,200 per arm and the MDE falls from 2.79pt to 1.60pt (MDE scales as 1/sqrt(n): 2.79 x sqrt(1400/4200) = 1.60), which is inside the range of a real framing effect.
tests.decisionRule: Pre-register a THREE-EDITION sequential test now, with one pre-specified read after Horizon VI and none before. Freeze the salt, the two copy blocks and the endpoint in writing today. Interim rule: after each edition publish the per-arm registration rate with its 95% CI and the running pooled estimate, and explicitly label it 'insufficient, do not act'. Final rule after edition three: winner requires p<0.05 and >= 1.6pt at pooled n. If it is still null after three editions, the conclusion is 'framing does not move registration by more than 1.6pt on this audience', which is a genuinely useful finding and should end the debate rather than restart it.

tests.stage: Stage 6 (T+1, Thank you + recording + next edition)
tests.hypothesis: Because the audience is clinicians reading on personal free-mail accounts and the brief's own copy library moves toward plain conversational notes, we believe a plain unstyled email that looks like it came from a colleague will cause a higher click rate on the recording link than a designed HTML layout, measured by reliableClicks/delivered.
tests.variantA: Designed: header band, logo, faculty photos, styled button, footer with the five-link social block from the June drafts.
tests.variantB: Plain: black text on white, system font, no images except the mandatory 1x1 tracking pixel, no social block, inline link, signature only.
tests.primaryMetric: Unique HUMAN click rate on the recording link.
tests.guardrailMetric: Unsubscribe rate per arm and complaint rate <0.100%. Also compare the PROXY and BOT open shares between arms from GET /api/analytics/classifier: an image-heavy arm interacts differently with Gmail and Yahoo image proxies, and the classifier only counts a proxy fetch as HUMAN outside the 3-second prefetch window, so a design difference can move the measured open rate without any human behaviour changing at all.
tests.sampleSizeMath: Post-event audience approx 2,760, 1,380 per arm. Recording-link click base on a post-event mail is high, call it 8%. Required to detect 8% -> 11% (3pt, +38% relative): 7.849 x (0.0736 + 0.0979) / 0.0009 = 1,496 per arm = 2,992 delivered. We have 2,760. MISSES by 8%, which is close enough that a genuinely large plain-vs-designed effect would be visible. Achieved MDE at 1,380/arm on an 8% base = 3.1pt. Important measurement note: both arms are still HTML as far as SesSender is concerned (it always builds an HTML body and injects the pixel when trackOpens is on), so the open pixel fires in both and open rates ARE comparable here. A true text/plain arm would have no pixel at all and would make the open comparison meaningless, which is a reason not to build one.
tests.decisionRule: Borderline, so treat as directional-with-teeth. Read at 96h. If plain beats designed by >= 3.1pt on clicks with p<0.05, switch the whole Horizon V sequence to plain and drop the design work permanently, which is a large operational saving. If the gap is smaller than 3.1pt in either direction, the pre-registered action is to adopt PLAIN anyway on cost grounds and note that the test could not distinguish them. Say that out loud in the readout so nobody later cites this as evidence that plain wins.

tests.stage: Spacing between Stage 3 (T-9) and Stage 4 (T-4) - independent persistent salt, arms receive Stage 4 on different dates
tests.hypothesis: Because the two June flows were drafted with 4 to 7 day gaps and the strategy brief separately imposes a 3-emails-per-contact-per-7-days cap, we believe a tighter 3-day gap before the final reminder will cause more registrations without a material unsubscribe penalty, measured by cumulative registration rate and unsubscribe rate per arm.
tests.variantA: 6-day gap: Stage 3 at T-9, Stage 4 at T-3.
tests.variantB: 3-day gap: Stage 3 at T-9, an added nudge at T-6, Stage 4 at T-3 (three touches in the final week, at the cap).
tests.primaryMetric: Cumulative registration rate by event day (Zoom export joined on email to arm assignment).
tests.guardrailMetric: THIS IS THE TEST WHERE THE GUARDRAIL MATTERS MORE THAN THE PRIMARY. Unsubscribe rate per arm, complaint rate which must stay below 0.100% per arm (SafetyCheckService hard-blocks the next send at 0.5% complaint / 5% bounce, so a bad result here can take the whole programme offline), and total suppression growth. Stop the tight arm immediately at 0.15% complaint.
tests.sampleSizeMath: 1,400 per arm. Cumulative registration base 6%. Required to detect 6% -> 8%: 2,551 per arm = 5,102 delivered, 1.5x the roster. FAILS by 1.8x. On the guardrail side it is worse: unsubscribe base is roughly 0.3% per send, and detecting a 0.2pt difference (0.3% -> 0.5%) needs 7.849 x (0.00299 + 0.004975) / 0.000004 = 15,630 per arm, 9x the roster. So this test can neither confirm the registration gain nor rule out the unsubscribe cost at conventional standards. The 95% CI on the registration difference at this n is +/-1.76pt.
tests.decisionRule: Run it, but govern it as a risk experiment rather than a significance test. Pre-registered stopping rule that fires on raw counts, not p-values: if the tight arm's cumulative unsubscribes exceed the slow arm's by more than 15 people (roughly 1.1pt on 1,400), abandon the tight cadence immediately and do not run Stage 4 for that arm. If complaints in the tight arm reach 2 people (0.14%), stop the arm the same hour. On the upside, adopt the tight cadence for Horizon V only if it leads registrations by more than 1.76pt AND its unsubscribe rate is within 0.3pt of the slow arm. Otherwise keep the 6-day gap and repeat the test in Horizon V with the same arms so the two editions pool to 2,800 per arm and the registration MDE drops from 2.79pt to 1.97pt.

honestLimits: The list is 3,363 addresses (verified: horizon-clean.csv, 3,363 data rows, all unique, 12 blank first names, 167 domains, 92.1% free-mail). After a 10% holdout and an assumed 6% first-send bounce on a new sending domain, a two-arm test has about 1,400 delivered per arm. That single number decides everything below. At 1,400 per arm and a 30% open baseline, the minimum detectable difference is 4.95 percentage points. Anything smaller than that is not a result, it is a coin flip with a chart on it.

Of the 11 tests here, exactly 3 are honestly powered: HZN-T0 (holdout, and only if email really is doing most of the work), HZN-T1 (sender identity, which fits with 3% headroom), and arguably HZN-T2 (subject framing, which fits on paper and then fails the moment Apple MPP is accounted for). The other 8 are underpowered by factors of 1.5x to 9x and I have marked every one of them rather than dressing them up.

Named explicitly, because this is the part that usually gets fudged: HZN-T3 (send time) needs 8,390 per arm to see a realistic 2pt effect and has 1,400, a 6x shortfall. HZN-T4 (length) needs 5,298 per arm for a 1pt click move and has 1,400, a 3.8x shortfall. HZN-T5 (button vs link) is powered only to detect a DOUBLING of click rate, which no button has ever produced. HZN-T7 (personalisation) needs 9,536 per arm and has 1,380, a 7x shortfall. HZN-T8 (proof vs mission) needs 2,551 and has 1,390. HZN-T10 (gap length) needs 2,551 for the registration read and 15,630 for the unsubscribe read, and has 1,400. HZN-T9 (plain vs designed) is the only near-miss, at 1,496 needed versus 1,380 available.

A 2-point open-rate difference at 1,400 per arm carries a 95% confidence interval of plus or minus 3.39 points. It contains zero. Calling it a winner is not a judgement call, it is arithmetically wrong, and the campaign that gets promoted on that basis will regress to the mean at the next send and be blamed on 'list fatigue'.

Apple MPP quietly halves the value of every open-based test on this list. The classifier is good (it flags bare AppleWebKit user agents plus Apple's 17.0.0.0/8 range), but flagging is the same as discarding for the purpose of a rate: a person whose only open is MPP counts as a non-opener. That is balanced across arms so it does not bias the comparison, but it shrinks the measured effect by roughly the MPP share. If 25% of true openers are hidden, a genuine 5-point subject-line lift shows up as 3.75 points on a 22.5% base and needs 2,054 per arm, which this list does not have. Read mppOpens from GET /api/analytics/classifier on the first send BEFORE committing to any open-based decision rule.

There is no conversion tracking at all. GET /api/mailer/success is a static thank-you page that records nothing, and there is no inbound API for a registration system to post back. Every registration metric in this programme is produced by exporting the Zoom registrant list after the event and joining it on lowercased email to the arm assignment CSV, by hand, offline. That works and it is deterministic, but it is a manual step that will be skipped under time pressure, and if it is skipped the entire programme reduces to open and click theatre.

There is no reply detection, so HZN-T6 is unmeasurable and I have marked it skip rather than pretending. Reply rate is probably the single most predictive metric for clinician webinar attendance, and it is the one this platform cannot see.

Running 11 tests at alpha 0.05 gives roughly a 43% chance of at least one false positive if every effect is truly zero. Correcting for that (Bonferroni to alpha 0.0045) multiplies every required n by 1.73 and every MDE by 1.32, which would push even the sender-identity test out of reach. The resolution is not to correct: it is to pre-register exactly THREE confirmatory tests (T0, T1, T2) at alpha 0.05 and declare the remaining eight exploratory with no significance claims permitted, ever, in any readout.

No baseline exists. There is not a single open rate, click rate, bounce rate, complaint rate or delivery count anywhere on this machine for any JCF send. The 25-35% open and 2-4% click assumptions used in every calculation above are category priors, not measurements. The June send went out through Postmark and its stats live in a dashboard nobody has exported. Every n in this document should be recomputed after the first JCF-Mailer send produces real numbers, and the first send should be treated as a calibration run, not as evidence.

The bounce assumption is load-bearing and unverified. This list was last mailed in June from a different ESP on a different domain, and 92.1% of it is free-mail. A 6% bounce rate is optimistic for that profile; 10-12% is possible, which would drop delivered to about 2,700 and push even HZN-T1 to the edge. Worse, the SNS webhook is inert (jarurat.sns.allowed-topic-arns is unset, so every POST /api/sns/ses-events returns 403) and aws.ses.configurationSet is blank, so per-message bounce events are not being published at all. The only live signal is the 15-minute SES suppression-list poll, which is account-level and attributes bounces to campaigns by an email-plus-timestamp heuristic that the code itself documents as over-counting when two campaigns mailed the same address. With four arm campaigns per stage mailing overlapping windows, that heuristic will over-count in every arm. Fix the configuration set and the SNS topic ARN before the first test send, or per-arm bounce numbers are fiction.

The four-cell stages are hand-built. There is no variant support in the platform, so every stage of this programme means creating 2 or 4 separate campaigns, 2 or 4 separate static lists, and 2 or 4 separate CSV imports, then reading 4 separate analytics endpoints. That is roughly 20 campaigns and 8 lists for one edition. The failure mode is not statistical, it is operational: someone pastes the wrong body into the wrong cell at 11pm and the whole edition's data is void with no way to detect it after the fact. Build the QA checklist (GET /api/campaigns/{id}/rendered on every cell, diffed against the intended copy, before any send) and treat it as non-optional.

The genuinely correct answer for a 3,363-person list is not a bigger test programme, it is fewer tests with bigger swings. Two arms, one factor, whole list, an effect you actually expect to be 5 points or more, repeated identically across three editions with a single pre-registered read at the end. Everything else on this list is intellectual furniture, and I would rather say so now than produce a deck of green checkmarks in October.
teachingNotes: BUCKETING, since the platform has none. Assign offline, before import, with SHA-256: arm = int(sha256(salt + ':' + lower(trim(email))).hexdigest()[:8], 16) % 2. Keyed on the lowercased email, never on a database id, because subscriber ids are assigned at import and would change if the list is ever re-imported. The salt is the experiment key, one fixed string per test (HZN-S1-SENDER, HZN-S2-SUBJECT, HZN-S3-TIME, and so on), never the campaign id, so the same person lands in the same arm at every stage of the sequence and across editions. I ran this on the real file: HZN-S1-SENDER splits 1,744 / 1,619 and HZN-S2-SUBJECT splits 1,681 / 1,682.

ORTHOGONALITY IS FREE AND IT IS THE WHOLE TRICK ON A SMALL LIST. Because each test uses an independent salt, the arms of test 2 are automatically balanced on exposure to test 1. Verified on the real file: the S1 x S2 cross-tab came out 846 / 898 / 835 / 784. That means a 2x2 factorial stage estimates each main effect at the FULL half-list n (about 1,400 per level) rather than at the cell n (about 700), which is the only way to run more than one test on 3,363 people. The cost is that you cannot read the interaction: at 700 per cell an interaction needs roughly 4x the main-effect sample. Pre-register that you will not look at interactions.

Do not use rank-based splitting (sort by hash, take the top half) even though it gives an exactly balanced 50/50. It is not stable: adding or removing a single address reshuffles everyone near the median, which breaks arm persistence across stages. Hash-mod is stable under roster changes and the imbalance costs almost nothing. On the real 3,363 the worst observed split (1,744/1,619) has a harmonic effective n of 1,679 against 1,681 for a perfect split, a power loss under 0.2%.

CAP CONCURRENT FACTORS AT TWO. Three factors plus a persistent sender frame means 8 hand-built campaigns and 8 hand-built lists per stage, and the operational error rate will exceed the effect you are measuring.

MAP ARMS ONTO THE PLATFORM AS SEPARATE CAMPAIGNS. One static list per arm (POST /api/lists then POST /api/lists/import with the arm CSV), one campaign per arm per stage, naming convention HZN4-S2-T1b-T2a so the cell is readable from GET /api/campaigns. The payoff is that AnalyticsService.byCampaign then IS per-variant analytics for free, with no code change. Schedule every cell of a stage at the SAME scheduledAt minute, except in the deliberate send-time test, or arm is confounded with send hour.

READ THE CLASSIFIED ENDPOINT, NOT THE LEGACY ONE. GET /api/analytics/summary?campaignId= gives reliableOpens (unique HUMAN) over delivered. GET /api/campaigns and GET /api/overview report the legacy inflated rate computed from CampaignRecipient.openedAt, which counts bots and Apple MPP. The summary response even hands you inflationFactor so you can see how wrong the old number is. Pick one stack on day one, write it into the pre-registration, and never mix the two in a single comparison.

THE TEST. Two-proportion z-test: z = (p2 - p1) / sqrt(p_pool(1-p_pool)(1/n1 + 1/n2)). Sample size: n per arm = 7.849 x [p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)] / (p2-p1)^2, where 7.849 = (1.96 + 0.8416)^2 for two-sided alpha 0.05 and 80% power. Worked example used throughout: p1 = 0.30, p2 = 0.35 gives 7.849 x (0.21 + 0.2275) / 0.0025 = 1,374 per arm, 2,748 total. Reference points for other list sizes, since the question asked: at 30% baseline and 5pt MDE a 500-person list is 5.5x too small, a 2,000-person list is 1.4x too small, and 5,000 is the first size at which the test comfortably fits (and even then only for a 5pt effect, not a 2pt one).

REPEATING A TEST ACROSS STAGES DOES NOT INCREASE n. Five stages to the same 1,400 people is 7,000 observations but still 1,400 independent subjects, and treating email-level opens as independent samples is the most common way small-list A/B programmes manufacture false winners. Always collapse to one row per person per arm, using a cumulative endpoint: opened at least one of stages 1-5, clicked at least once, registered by event day. Cumulative endpoints also have higher base rates, which shrinks the relative MDE for free.

SEQUENTIAL LEARNING ACROSS EDITIONS IS THE REAL PROGRAMME. Same salts, same arms, same copy contrast, repeated across Horizon IV, V and VI, with ONE pre-registered read at the end. Three editions pool to about 4,200 per arm and MDE scales as 1/sqrt(n): a 2.79pt MDE at 1,400 becomes 1.60pt at 4,200. That is the difference between never being able to answer the proof-vs-mission question and answering it in nine months. It only works if the arms are frozen now, in writing, before anyone sees a number.

PRE-REGISTER BEFORE THE SEND, IN A FILE, WITH A TIMESTAMP. Primary metric, guardrail metric, exact read time, exact decision threshold, and the action on a null result. The null action is the field everyone skips and it is the one that prevents the post-hoc story. One look per test at a fixed time. No dashboard-watching at 6 hours, because a mid-flight peek at a nominally significant gap converts alpha 0.05 into something closer to 0.20.

GUARDRAILS ARE HARD STOPS, NOT METRICS. Complaint rate above 0.100% and bounce rate above 2.00% are the platform's own danger lines; SafetyCheckService hard-blocks a send at 5.0% bounce or 0.5% complaint, so a reckless cadence arm can take the entire programme offline mid-sequence. In the cadence test the stopping rule fires on raw counts (15 excess unsubscribes, 2 complaints), not on p-values, because you cannot afford to wait for significance on a reputational risk.

FIX THREE PLATFORM THINGS BEFORE THE FIRST TEST SEND, all cheap. (1) Set aws.ses.configurationSet and jarurat.sns.allowed-topic-arns, otherwise SES publishes no per-message events and the SNS webhook 403s on every payload, leaving bounce attribution to a heuristic the code itself documents as over-counting. (2) Exclude or fill the 12 blank first names, because applyMergeFields blanks unresolved tokens and would ship 'Dear ,'. (3) Add the pg advisory lock to runDueCampaigns, a two-line fix, because with four campaigns scheduled at the same minute across two instances the double-send risk stops being theoretical.

THREE BUILDS WOULD CHANGE THE ECONOMICS, in priority order. (a) Conversion tracking, marked small in the audit: accept ?token= on GET /api/mailer/success and add POST /api/v1/conversions to the existing API-key-authed controller. This removes the manual Zoom-join step that every registration metric in this programme currently depends on. (b) VERP reply capture, marked medium: a per-recipient Reply-To of reply+{token}@jarurat.care plus a scheduled scanner with its own credential. Reply rate is the best available proxy for clinician intent and is currently invisible. (c) The variant dimension, marked medium: a variant_key column on campaign_recipient and tracking_event plus a VariantAssigner. Worth it only after (a) and (b), because the separate-campaign workaround already delivers per-arm analytics, whereas nothing at all delivers conversions or replies.
